## Warm hands, warmer judgments?

Holding something warm can bias how "warm" or trustworthy another person feels. The brain region often discussed is the **anterior insular cortex**, which handles both physical temperature and social feelings. Effects on real choices are real in some studies—but not magic, and not always easy to replicate.

Williams and Bargh (2008) reported that people who briefly held a warm cup of coffee rated a stranger as having a "warmer" personality than people who held an iced cup, and that holding a warm (versus cold) therapeutic pad raised the chance of choosing a gift for a friend rather than for oneself [^1]. Follow-on work linked physical and social "warmth" in the insula [^2]. Kang and colleagues reported that physical temperature also shifted responses to fairness in bargaining games [^3].

| Condition | Stimulus | Typical behavioral skew in cited work | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warm prime | Warm insulated cup / hot coffee briefly held | Partners rated warmer/more trustworthy; more friend-oriented gift choice in original Study 2 | Williams & Bargh (2008) [^1] |
| Cold prime | Iced cup / cold pad | Partners framed as colder/distant; more self-oriented choice | Williams & Bargh (2008); Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013) [^1][^2] |
| Warm mug in Trust / fairness settings | Warm ~60°C mug (pack narrative of Kang et al.) | Higher first-mover investment / fairness sensitivity in cited designs | Kang et al. (2011) [^3] |

You meet someone while holding a cozy mug versus an icy can. In some lab setups, that body feeling spills into how "warm" the person seems. That is the embodied-cognition idea in everyday clothes.

Study snapshots from the packs and the papers:

- Warm vs cold mug: personality "warmth" ratings about **5.63** vs **4.04** on a 1–7 scale (Williams & Bargh, 2008) [^1].  
- Gift choice: warm prime **54%** chose a gift for a friend; cold prime **75%** chose for self (same paper) [^1].  
- Trust Game: warm mug (~60°C) raised first-mover investment about **+24.8%** vs cold pad (Kang et al., 2011; pack narrative) [^3].  

A warm cup can nudge first impressions and opening trust in cited work. It does not guarantee generosity forever, and one famous behavioral result did not copy cleanly in a large replication.

People sometimes say: "Warm mug always makes people generous." Williams & Bargh (2008) reported a very large effect. A large preregistered multi-lab replication of Study 2 (Lynott et al., 2014; total N = 861) failed to copy the pure behavioral gift-choice result [^4]. Later independent replications have also reported near-zero effects for the original warmth-to-prosocial link [^5]. Overlap between physical warmth and social bonding in the insula looks more robust in neuroimaging designs [^2]; outward behavior depends on person and setting. That honesty is part of the story: interesting claim, checked claim, limited claim.

This warmth thread will reappear in Chapter 4's Trust Game—the same first-mover figure is one of the bridges on [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: warmth priming results—and what failed to replicate"}
| Condition | Stimulus | Behavioral skew in cited work | Trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warm prime | Warm cup / hot coffee briefly held | "Warmer" personality ratings; more friend-oriented gift choice in original Study 2 | Williams & Bargh (2008)[^1] |
| Cold prime | Iced cup / cold pad | Colder/distant framing; more self-oriented choice | Williams & Bargh; Inagaki & Eisenberger[^1][^2] |
| Warm mug in fairness / trust settings | Warm ~**60°C** mug (pack narrative of Kang et al.) | Higher first-mover investment / fairness sensitivity in cited designs | Kang et al. (2011)[^3] |

Snapshots: warmth ratings about **5.63** vs **4.04** (1–7); gift choice warm **54%** friend vs cold **75%** self; Trust Game first-mover investment about **+24.8%** warm vs cold (pack narrative of Kang).[^1][^3]

**Replication honesty.** A large preregistered multi-lab replication of Williams & Bargh Study 2 (Lynott et al., 2014; N = 861) **failed** to copy the pure behavioral gift-choice result.[^4] Later independent reports have also found near-zero effects for the original warmth-to-prosocial link.[^5] Insula overlap between physical and social warmth looks more robust in neuroimaging designs;[^2] outward behavior depends on person and setting. Interesting claim → checked claim → limited claim.
:::

Warmth is passive. Ritual is active. What happens when you *make* the tea on purpose?

[^2]: Inagaki, T. K., & Eisenberger, N. I. (2013). Shared neural mechanisms underlying social warmth and physical warmth. *Psychological Science, 24*(11), 2272–2280.

[^3]: Kang, Y., Williams, L. E., Clark, M. S., Gray, J. R., & Bargh, J. A. (2011). Physical temperature affects response to fairness. *PLOS ONE, 6*(1), e15836. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015836

[^4]: Lynott, D., et al. (2014). Replication of "Experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth" by Williams and Bargh (2008). *Social Psychology, 45*(3), 216–222. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000187

[^5]: Chabris, C. F., et al. (2018 preprint / later reports). Failures to replicate Williams and Bargh (2008) warmth priming in field settings. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/mvn9b
